section.title: Wanderings in the Wilderness
section.sectionRationale: Moses continues the historical review, tracing Israel's long detour around Edom, Moab, and Ammon before the first great victory over Sihon, showing that the same LORD who governs Israel's inheritance also governs the boundaries of every nation.
section.thesis: As Israel's forty years of wandering draw to a close, Moses recounts how the LORD scrupulously honored the God-given lands of Edom, Moab, and Ammon, and then hardened Sihon's heart to bring about the first great victory that would embolden Israel for the conquest ahead.
section.frameNote: Five movements: passing by Edom in peace; passing by Moab, with a note on the peoples God displaced before them; passing by Ammon, with a similar note; the command to engage Sihon; and Sihon's refusal, defeat, and total destruction.

verses.text: Then we turned back and headed for the wilderness by way of the Red Sea, as the LORD had instructed me, and for many days we wandered around Mount Seir.
At this time the LORD said to me,
“You have been wandering around this hill country long enough; turn to the north
and command the people: ‘You will pass through the territory of your brothers, the descendants of Esau, who live in Seir. They will be afraid of you, so you must be very careful.
Do not provoke them, for I will not give you any of their land, not even a footprint, because I have given Mount Seir to Esau as his {{yerushah|possession}}.
You are to pay them in silver for the food you eat and the water you drink.’”

Indeed, the LORD your God has blessed you in all the work of your hands. He has watched over your journey through this vast wilderness. The LORD your God has been with you these forty years, and you have lacked nothing.

So we passed by our brothers, the descendants of Esau, who live in Seir. We turned away from the Arabah road, which comes up from Elath and Ezion-geber, and traveled along the road of the Wilderness of Moab.

units.label: Passing by Moab
units.note: the LORD's providence over every nation

verses.text: Then the LORD said to me, “Do not harass the Moabites or provoke them to war, for I will not give you any of their land, because I have given Ar to the descendants of Lot as their possession.”
(The Emites used to live there, a people great and many, as tall as the Anakites.
Like the Anakites, they were also regarded as Rephaim, though the Moabites called them Emites.

The Horites used to live in Seir, but the descendants of Esau drove them out. They destroyed the Horites from before them and settled in their place, just as Israel did in the land that the LORD gave them as their possession.)
“Now arise and cross over the Brook of Zered.” So we crossed over the Brook of Zered.

The time we spent traveling from Kadesh-barnea until we crossed over the Brook of Zered was thirty-eight years, until that entire generation of fighting men had perished from the camp, as the LORD had sworn to them.
Indeed, the LORD's hand was against them, to eliminate them from the camp, until they had all perished.
Now when all the fighting men among the people had died,
the LORD said to me,
“Today you are going to cross the border of Moab at Ar.
But when you get close to the Ammonites, do not harass them or provoke them, for I will not give you any of the land of the Ammonites. I have given it to the descendants of Lot as their possession.”
(That too was regarded as the land of the Rephaim, who used to live there, though the Ammonites called them Zamzummites.
They were a people great and many, as tall as the Anakites. But the LORD destroyed them from before the Ammonites, who drove them out and settled in their place,
just as He had done for the descendants of Esau who lived in Seir, when He destroyed the Horites from before them. They drove them out and have lived in their place to this day.
And the Avvim, who lived in villages as far as Gaza, were destroyed by the Caphtorites, who came out of Caphtor and settled in their place.)

units.label: The command to engage Sihon
units.note: I have delivered him into your hand

verses.text: “Arise, set out, and cross the Arnon Valley. See, I have delivered into your hand Sihon the Amorite, king of Heshbon, and his land. Begin to take possession of it and engage him in battle.
This very day I will begin to put the dread and fear of you upon all the nations under heaven. They will hear the reports of you and tremble in anguish because of you.”
So from the Wilderness of Kedemoth I sent messengers with an offer of peace to Sihon king of Heshbon, saying,
“Let us pass through your land; we will stay on the main road. We will not turn to the right or to the left.
You can sell us food to eat and water to drink in exchange for silver. Only let us pass through on foot,
just as the descendants of Esau who live in Seir and the Moabites who live in Ar did for us, until we cross the Jordan into the land that the LORD our God is giving us.”

But Sihon king of Heshbon would not let us pass through, for the LORD your God had made his spirit {{qashah|stubborn}} and his heart obstinate, that He might deliver him into your hand, as is the case this day.
Then the LORD said to me, “See, I have begun to deliver Sihon and his land over to you. Now begin to conquer and possess his land.”
So Sihon and his whole army came out for battle against us at Jahaz.
And the LORD our God delivered him over to us, and we defeated him and his sons and his whole army.
At that time we captured all his cities and devoted to destruction the people of every city, including women and children. We left no survivors.
We carried off for ourselves only the livestock and the plunder from the cities we captured.
From Aroer on the rim of the Arnon Valley, along with the city in the valley, even as far as Gilead, not one city had walls too high for us. The LORD our God gave us all of them.
But you did not go near the land of the Ammonites, or the land along the banks of the Jabbok River, or the cities of the hill country, or any place that the LORD our God had forbidden.

yerushah.gloss: Possession, inheritance. The same word used for Israel's inheritance of Canaan is applied here to Esau's, Moab's, and Ammon's lands, showing that the LORD who apportions Israel's inheritance also apportions the boundaries of every nation, Acts 17:26.

qashah.gloss: To be hard, stubborn, obstinate. Used of Sihon's spirit here just as Pharaoh's heart is hardened in Exodus, describing God's sovereign hand working through, not against, genuine human stubbornness to bring about His purposes.

basic.context: Moses continues retelling the wilderness years: Israel's long, obedient detour around the lands of Edom, Moab, and Ammon, God's kinsmen through Esau and Lot, followed by the command to engage and defeat Sihon, the first Amorite king blocking their path to the land.
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative retold to show two things at once: God's fairness toward nations outside Israel's covenant, and His sovereign hand in bringing about Israel's first victory. It is descriptive of a specific redemptive-historical moment, not a manual for handling every neighboring nation today.
basic.originalLanguages: The word for Esau's, Moab's, and Ammon's lands is yerushah, possession or inheritance, the same word used for Israel's own inheritance of Canaan, underlining that the LORD governs every nation's boundaries. Sihon's refusal comes because the LORD made his spirit qashah, stubborn, echoing the hardening of Pharaoh's heart in Exodus.
basic.typology: The pattern of God hardening a hostile ruler's heart to bring about a greater deliverance recalls Pharaoh and anticipates how God works even through human resistance and evil intentions to accomplish His redemptive purposes, climactically at the cross, Acts 2:23.
basic.christ: Sihon's total defeat becomes the first fulfillment of the LORD's promise to fight for Israel, a pattern that finds its ultimate expression in Christ's victory over every hostile power, Colossians 2:15, where even the wrath of His enemies serves to accomplish God's saving plan.
basic.god: God is scrupulously just, honoring the land grants He made to Edom, Moab, and Ammon even though they are outside His covenant with Israel; He is also sovereign over hardened hearts, using even Sihon's stubbornness to advance His purposes for His people.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 4:21 and 7:3 describe the LORD hardening Pharaoh's heart in a similar way. Acts 17:26 says God determined the boundaries of every nation. Numbers 21:21-30 gives the parallel account of Sihon's defeat.
basic.oneStory: This chapter shows the God of Israel as Lord over every nation's borders and every ruler's heart, whether friendly like Edom or hostile like Sihon. The same sovereign hand that measured out the nations' lands now begins to clear the way for Israel's inheritance, foreshadowing the greater victory Christ wins over every hostile power.

context.literary:
Chapter 2 picks up exactly where chapter 1 left Israel, turning back toward the Red Sea road, verse 1, as God had ordered in 1:40. Then comes a divine word that echoes the opening of the book: 'You have been wandering around this hill country long enough,' verse 3, matching 'You have stayed at this mountain long enough,' 1:6. The long pause is over, and the journey resumes.

The chapter is built from three encounters of restraint followed by one of conquest. Edom, verses 4 to 8, Moab, verses 9 to 13, and Ammon, verses 16 to 23, each receive a matching pattern: a command not to provoke, a refusal of land, and a reason, 'I have given' it to them 'as their possession.' Sihon, verses 24 to 37, then receives the opposite command, to 'engage him in battle.' The contrast is the point. Israel's restraint and Israel's warfare both come from the same word of God.

Twice the narrative breaks into parentheses, verses 10 to 12 and 20 to 23, with notes on the peoples who lived in these lands before: Emites, Horites, Zamzummites, Avvim. These antiquarian asides are not digressions. They show that the displacement of giants is something God has done for other nations too, which makes the Anakim who terrified the first generation look far less invincible.

At the centre stands a hinge, verses 14 to 16. The crossing of the Zered marks the end of thirty-eight years, 'until that entire generation of fighting men had perished.' Only after that notice does the language of battle begin. Three times in the Sihon section God speaks of beginning, 'Begin to take possession,' verse 24, 'This very day I will begin,' verse 25, and 'I have begun to deliver,' verse 31. The generation of wandering is finished, and the generation of conquest starts here.
context.historical:
The route runs north along the eastern edge of the Arabah, the rift valley south of the Dead Sea. Israel skirts Edom, whose heartland was the high country of Seir, then crosses the Brook of Zered, the traditional border between Edom and Moab, usually identified with the Wadi al-Hasa. It continues past Moab, whose northern border was the Arnon, the deep gorge usually identified with the Wadi Mujib, and approaches Ammon, whose western frontier followed the upper Jabbok. The main road the messengers mention, verse 27, is called 'the King's Highway' in the parallel accounts, Numbers 20:17 and 21:22.

The three peoples Israel must leave alone are relatives. Esau, that is Edom, settled in Mount Seir, Genesis 36:8. Moab and Ammon descend from Lot's two sons, Genesis 19:36-38. Moses calls the Edomites 'your brothers,' verse 4, and the law later says, 'Do not despise an Edomite, for he is your brother,' Deuteronomy 23:7.

The parenthetical notes preserve old ethnic memories. The Emites, Horites and Rephaim appear together in Genesis 14:5-6, where Chedorlaomer's coalition defeats them. The Caphtorites came 'out of Caphtor,' which the BSB footnote identifies as Crete, and Amos 9:7 says the LORD brought 'the Philistines from Caphtor.'

Sihon's kingdom was itself a recent conquest. Numbers 21:26 notes that Sihon 'had fought against the former king of Moab and taken all his land as far as the Arnon.' So when Israel took Heshbon it did not violate the grant to Moab; it took land Moab had already lost. Jephthah later makes exactly this argument to the Ammonites, Judges 11:15-26, adding that Israel had held the region for three hundred years. The ancient reader would also have heard 'devoted to destruction,' verse 34, as the language of cherem, which the BSB footnote explains as giving persons or things over to the LORD.
context.canonical:
The Transjordan journey is told three times in the Old Testament, and the comparisons illuminate each other. Numbers 20:14-21 records Edom's refusal of passage from Kadesh, and Numbers 21:21-35 the victories over Sihon and Og. Judges 11:12-28 uses the history in diplomacy, with Jephthah insisting that Israel never took land from Moab or Ammon. Deuteronomy's version is shaped for preaching: it stresses God's gifts to other nations and His initiative against Sihon.

The victory over Sihon becomes a fixed point in Israel's memory. Rahab tells the spies that Canaan has heard 'what you did to Sihon and Og, the two kings of the Amorites,' Joshua 2:10, and the Gibeonites say the same, Joshua 9:10. Moses uses it to steady Joshua, 'The LORD will do to them as He did to Sihon and Og,' Deuteronomy 31:4. Psalm 135:10-12 and Psalm 136:17-22 sing it, and Psalm 136 answers each line with 'His loving devotion endures forever.' Nehemiah 9:21-22 joins the provision of the wilderness, 'they lacked nothing,' to the gift of Sihon's land in a single prayer of confession.

The relationship with Edom, Moab and Ammon runs through the rest of the canon. Ruth the Moabitess enters Israel and the line of David, Ruth 1:4 and Matthew 1:5. Obadiah condemns Edom for 'violence against your brother Jacob,' Obadiah 10, the brotherhood of Deuteronomy 2:4 turned to betrayal. Jeremiah promises that the LORD will restore Moab and Ammon 'in the latter days,' Jeremiah 48:47 and 49:6.

The New Testament takes up the principle that God allots nations their lands. Paul tells the Athenians that God 'determined their appointed times and the boundaries of their lands,' Acts 17:26, and adds the purpose, that they 'would seek Him.' The hardening of Sihon, like that of Pharaoh, stands behind Paul's argument in Romans 9:17-18.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wants the new generation to understand that the war they are about to fight is not a war of greed. The same God who is giving them Canaan has told them to walk past fertile, reachable land because He has given it to others, 'not even a footprint,' verse 5. Their restraint toward Edom, Moab and Ammon is evidence that their conquest is governed by God's word and not by their appetite.

He also wants them to see that the long sentence of chapter 1 has been fully served. Verses 14 to 16 state it three ways: the generation 'had perished,' the LORD's hand was against them 'until they had all perished,' and 'when all the fighting men among the people had died.' The emphasis is sobering and freeing at once. God did exactly what He swore, and now He is ready to do what He promised.

Finally, Moses wants them to face Canaan without the fear that paralysed their parents. The notes about the Rephaim and the Anakim are aimed at that fear. Other nations have displaced giants, verses 10 to 12 and 20 to 22. Sihon was defeated, and 'not one city had walls too high for us,' verse 36, a pointed answer to the report of cities 'with walls up to the heavens,' 1:28.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes a unique stage in Israel's history, and much of it cannot be carried directly into the present. God's specific grants of land to Edom, Moab and Ammon, and His command to destroy Sihon's cities, belong to a particular moment in the story of redemption. They are not a charter for modern states to claim territory or wage war in God's name, and Jesus says plainly that His servants do not fight to establish His kingdom, John 18:36.

Some things in the chapter do instruct directly. Israel's conduct toward its neighbours models integrity: paying in silver for food and water, verse 6, staying on the road, verse 27, and offering peace before any conflict, verse 26. The law later makes the offer of peace a standing rule for warfare, Deuteronomy 20:10, and the New Testament asks believers, 'If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone,' Romans 12:18.

The theological claims apply without adjustment. God gives nations their places, Acts 17:26, and He rules over the hearts of rulers, Romans 13:1. These are descriptions of His ongoing government, not only of what He once did east of the Jordan.

debates.question: Does God's hardening of Sihon's heart (verse 30) remove Sihon's own responsibility for refusing peace?

views.label: God's hardening works through real human choice
views.case: Scripture holds both truths together, as with Pharaoh. Exodus 9:12 says 'the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart,' while Exodus 8:15 says Pharaoh 'hardened his heart.' Sihon genuinely chose to refuse a fair offer, verses 26 to 29, and verse 32 shows him marching out to attack. God's purpose did not override his will; it ran through it.

views.label: The hardening is God's judgment on prior wickedness
views.case: Some read the hardening as God confirming Sihon in a hostility he already held, much as Romans 1:24 says God 'gave them over in the desires of their hearts.' Sihon had already seized Moabite land by force, Numbers 21:26, and the Amorites' iniquity had been accumulating since Genesis 15:16.

views.label: The hardening is a statement of sovereignty, without explaining how
views.case: Others note that the text gives the purpose, 'that He might deliver him into your hand,' but not the mechanism, and warn against resolving what Scripture leaves as a tension. Romans 9:18 states the same sovereignty without softening it: 'He hardens whom He wants to harden.'

debates.bearing: All three views agree that Sihon is accountable and that the outcome served God's purpose for Israel. The text is less interested in the mechanics than in reassuring Israel that the resistance ahead of them is not outside God's control.

debates.question: How can Israel devote Sihon's cities to destruction, 'including women and children' (verse 34)?

views.label: It is a unique act of divine judgment
views.case: The Amorites are singled out in Genesis 15:16, where God delays the conquest because 'the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete.' On this view the cherem is not Israel's policy but God's sentence, carried out once, at a particular time, against peoples whose guilt He had long endured. The same God judged Israel's own generation in the wilderness, verse 15.

views.label: It is a limited measure tied to the land and to idolatry
views.case: Deuteronomy 20:10-18 distinguishes distant cities, which are offered peace and spared, from the nations within the inheritance, and gives the reason: 'so that they cannot teach you to do all the detestable things they do for their gods.' Sihon was first offered peace, verse 26, and destruction followed only his attack.

views.label: The language reflects the conventions of ancient war reports
views.case: Some scholars argue that sweeping phrases such as 'we left no survivors' belong to a stylised way of reporting victory common in the ancient Near East, and that the texts should not be read as complete statistical accounts. They point out that later narratives in Joshua and Judges assume that many Canaanites remained.

debates.bearing: The first two views are complementary and closest to the text's own explanations: judgment on long-accumulated sin, limited to a particular moment and aimed at protecting Israel from idolatry. The third may soften the rhetoric but does not remove the moral question. The New Testament does not repeat the command; it points to the final judgment carried out by Christ Himself, 2 Thessalonians 1:7-8, with the offer of peace held open until then.

debates.question: Did Edom and Moab help Israel (verse 29), or refuse them (Numbers 20:14-21, Judges 11:17, Deuteronomy 23:4)?

views.label: Different routes and different moments
views.case: Numbers 20 describes a request made from Kadesh to cross Edom from the west, which the king refused. Deuteronomy 2 describes a later journey around the eastern edge of Seir, where the local descendants of Esau sold food and water, verse 29. Both can be true.

views.label: Official refusal, local trade
views.case: The kings of Edom and Moab refused passage through their heartlands, Judges 11:17, yet communities along the border traded with Israel for silver, verses 6 and 28 to 29. Deuteronomy 23:4 complains that Ammon and Moab 'did not meet you with food and water,' which may mean no hospitality was freely offered, even if supplies could be bought.

debates.bearing: Read together the texts show neither hostility nor friendship in a simple form. What Deuteronomy stresses is Israel's own conduct: they did not provoke, they paid their way, and they left the land God had given to others.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb translated 'provoke' in verses 5, 9 and 19 is garah in its reflexive stem, 'to stir oneself up to strife.' It appears in the Moab command with the fuller phrase 'provoke them to war,' verse 9. Then in verse 24 the same verb and the same noun reappear as a command: 'engage him in battle,' literally 'stir yourself up against him in war.' The vocabulary is deliberate. What God forbids against His gifts to Esau and Lot, He commands against Sihon. The morality of Israel's warfare lies not in the act but in the word that authorises or forbids it.

In verse 5 God refuses Israel 'not even a footprint' of Edom. The Hebrew is literally 'as much as the treading of the sole of a foot,' midrakh kaf ragel. The same imagery marks the promise to Israel: 'Every place where the sole of your foot treads will be yours,' Deuteronomy 11:24, repeated to Joshua in Joshua 1:3. The foot that is promised every step in Canaan is denied a single step in Seir. God's gifts have edges.

Verse 7 sums up the forty years: 'you have lacked nothing.' The verb is chaser, to lack or be in want. Deuteronomy 8:9 uses it for the land ahead, 'where you will lack nothing,' Nehemiah 9:21 uses it in prayer, 'they lacked nothing,' and Psalm 23:1 uses it in the most famous line of the Psalter, 'I shall not want.' The years of judgment were also years of full provision.

In verse 15 the LORD's hand was against the first generation 'to eliminate them.' The verb is hamam, which elsewhere describes the LORD throwing Israel's enemies into panic in holy war: He 'threw their camp into confusion' at the Red Sea, Exodus 14:24, promises to 'throw into confusion every nation you encounter,' Exodus 23:27, and did so at Gibeon, Joshua 10:10. Here the divine warrior's action is turned against His own unbelieving people. The judgment of the wilderness was holy war in reverse.

The verb 'begin,' from chalal in the causative stem, sounds three times in verses 24, 25 and 31. It marks a new era: after thirty-eight years of ending, God now begins. Moses will pick up the same verb in his prayer, 'You have begun to show Your greatness,' Deuteronomy 3:24.

Finally, 'devoted to destruction' in verse 34 translates the causative form of charam. The BSB footnote explains that cherem refers to 'the giving over of things or persons to the LORD, either by destroying them or by giving them as an offering.' Leviticus 27:28 shows the same idea in worship: whatever is devoted 'is most holy to the LORD' and cannot be redeemed. The word frames the conquest as an act belonging to God, not as plunder, which is why only livestock and goods could be kept, verse 35.

typology.type: Sihon hardened for judgment, echoing Pharaoh
typology.fulfillment: Sihon's refusal, like Pharaoh's, becomes the occasion for God to display His power and to deliver His people. Paul reads Pharaoh this way in Romans 9:17, 'I raised you up for this very purpose.' The pattern reaches its climax at the cross, where Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles and Israel 'carried out what Your hand and will had decided beforehand would happen,' Acts 4:27-28. The escalation is striking: at the cross the hostile powers did not only lose a battle, they became the instrument of the salvation they opposed. The type falls short because Sihon's defeat saved one nation, while Christ's death and resurrection open salvation to every nation.

typology.type: The offer of peace before judgment, verse 26
typology.fulfillment: Moses sent 'messengers with an offer of peace' before any battle, and judgment came only when the offer was refused. The same order governs the gospel. Christ 'came and preached peace to you who were far away and peace to those who were near,' Ephesians 2:17, and His apostles go out as ambassadors, 'Be reconciled to God,' 2 Corinthians 5:20. Jesus wept over Jerusalem, 'If only you had known on this day what would bring you peace!' Luke 19:42. The correspondence is real but the escalation is great, since the peace Christ offers is not safe passage on a road but reconciliation with God, and it is paid for by His own blood.

typology.type: The devoted destruction of Sihon's kingdom
typology.fulfillment: The cherem is the LORD fighting for His people and judging a hardened enemy, an early act of the holy war that runs through Scripture. The New Testament transposes that war. Christ 'disarmed the powers and authorities' and triumphed over them 'by the cross,' Colossians 2:15, and He will return as the rider called Faithful and True, who 'with righteousness judges and wages war,' Revelation 19:11. The type falls short and is transformed: the church's weapons are not swords against people, and the final judgment belongs to Christ alone, 2 Thessalonians 1:7-8.

typology.type: Forty years of provision in which Israel lacked nothing, verse 7
typology.fulfillment: The wilderness years were judgment on one generation and schooling for the next, and through them God supplied every need, Deuteronomy 29:5. Jesus reenacts the wilderness in forty days and answers the tempter from Deuteronomy 8:3, trusting His Father for bread, Matthew 4:1-4. He then becomes the provision Himself, the bread of life, John 6:35. The correspondence points believers to the same trust in the wilderness of this age, and the type falls short only because manna fed bodies for a season, while Christ gives life that does not end.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through the theme of nations and their places. God gave Seir to Esau and Ar to the descendants of Lot, verses 5 and 9, and He cared about their borders even though they were outside His covenant with Israel. That care is not incidental. It anticipates the promise that all nations would be blessed through Abraham's offspring, and the commission of the risen Christ to 'make disciples of all nations,' Matthew 28:19. Acts 17:26-27 joins the two ideas: God appointed the boundaries of the nations so that 'they would seek Him.' Moab, whom Israel was told not to harass, later gives Ruth to the line of David, and so to the genealogy of Jesus, Matthew 1:5.

It leads to Christ through the pattern of hostile rulers serving God's plan. Sihon is hardened 'that He might deliver him into your hand,' verse 30. The early church prayed with the same conviction after Jesus' death: 'They carried out what Your hand and will had decided beforehand would happen,' Acts 4:28. Peter preached that Jesus was 'delivered up by God's set plan and foreknowledge,' Acts 2:23. The difference is profound. Sihon was an enemy who deserved judgment; Jesus was the innocent Servant, and the evil done to Him became the means of forgiveness for the very people who did it, Luke 23:34.

It leads to Christ through the offer of peace. Israel asked only to pass through on the road, paying for food and water, verses 27 to 29. When that peace was refused, judgment followed. Christ comes as the one who 'preached peace,' Ephesians 2:17, and He warns that refusing the Son leaves God's wrath in place, John 3:36. The gospel is Deuteronomy 2:26 on a cosmic scale: an embassy of peace sent before the day of judgment.

It leads to Christ through the end of a generation. The first generation had to die in the wilderness before the second could cross into the land, verses 14 to 16. In Christ that death is borne for His people. Paul describes believers as those who have died with Christ and been raised with Him to walk in newness of life, Romans 6:4. The Zered crossing is not a baptism, and the chapter does not make it one, but it does show that God's people cannot enter the inheritance with the old unbelief still in charge.

Finally, the chapter points to Christ as the warrior who fights for His people. The victory over Sihon came because 'the LORD our God delivered him over to us,' verse 33. Colossians 2:15 declares the greater victory, Christ triumphing over the powers by the cross, and Revelation 19:11 the last one.
study.god:
The chapter shows God as the Lord of all the earth, not merely of Israel. He gives lands to Edom, Moab and Ammon, verses 5, 9 and 19. The parenthetical notes add that He also destroyed the Zamzummites 'from before the Ammonites,' verse 21, and did the same for Esau against the Horites, verse 22. The history of other peoples, their migrations and conquests, is under His hand. Even the Philistine settlement from Caphtor, verse 23, appears in Amos 9:7 as something God did.

He is faithful to His word in both directions. He had sworn that the Kadesh generation would die in the wilderness, and verses 14 to 16 record that He did it: 'the LORD's hand was against them.' He had promised the land to their children, and the same chapter records Him beginning to give it. The God who keeps His threats is the God who keeps His promises, and the second generation can trust the second because they have seen the first.

He is generous in judgment. The forty years were a sentence, yet 'the LORD your God has been with you these forty years, and you have lacked nothing,' verse 7. Discipline and provision ran side by side. God did not abandon the people He was judging.

He is just toward those outside the covenant. He tells Israel to pay in silver for food and water, verse 6, and forbids them to provoke peoples who might have been easy prey. Israel's strength is not permission to take. At the same time He is the judge of hardened wickedness, as Sihon learns. The God who protects Edom's borders is the God who overturns Sihon's kingdom, and both flow from the same righteousness.

He is sovereign over hearts. Verse 30 does not hide it: 'the LORD your God had made his spirit stubborn and his heart obstinate.' The chapter holds together God's rule and Sihon's guilt without resolving the tension, and it offers that sovereignty to Israel as comfort. Nothing that will oppose them lies outside His purpose.

For worship, the chapter invites us to trust God with our boundaries as well as our battles, to be content with what He gives, and to sing with Psalm 136 that in both provision and victory 'His loving devotion endures forever.'

crossReferences.note: Moses' earlier request to cross Edom from Kadesh, which Edom refused with an army. It sets the background for Deuteronomy 2:4-8 and explains why Israel went the long way round. Read together, the passages show Israel's patience with a brother nation even when rebuffed.

Numbers narrates the same battle at Jahaz but adds that Sihon had already taken Moab's land 'as far as the Arnon,' which explains how Israel could take Heshbon without breaking God's grant to the descendants of Lot, and it quotes an old victory song about Heshbon.

Jephthah's reply to the king of Ammon retells Deuteronomy 2 as a legal case. Israel bypassed Edom and Moab, took land from Sihon and not from Moab or Ammon, and had held it for three hundred years. It shows the chapter functioning as Israel's title deed.

The origin of Moab and Ammon from Lot's two sons. Deuteronomy 2:9 and 2:19 call them 'the descendants of Lot,' so the land grants of this chapter extend God's care from Abraham to his nephew's family, despite the shameful story of their beginning.

'Do not despise an Edomite, for he is your brother.' The law carries forward the brotherhood that governed Israel's conduct in Deuteronomy 2:4-8, and it shows that the restraint of the wilderness journey was meant to shape Israel's lasting attitude to Edom.

The law of warfare requires an offer of peace before attacking a city and distinguishes distant cities from those within the inheritance. Moses' offer of peace to Sihon, Deuteronomy 2:26, is that law in action, and the passage gives the reason for cherem: to keep Israel from idolatry.

Rahab tells the spies that Jericho has heard what Israel did to Sihon and Og, and 'our hearts melted.' The promise of Deuteronomy 2:25, that God would put the dread of Israel on the nations, is fulfilled, and it becomes the soil in which a Canaanite woman's faith grows.

Israel's worship sings the defeat of Sihon and Og line by line, answering each with 'His loving devotion endures forever.' The victory of Deuteronomy 2 is not remembered as military glory but as covenant love, God's chesed shown in the gift of an inheritance.

The returned exiles confess that God sustained Israel forty years 'so that they lacked nothing' and then gave them 'the land of Sihon king of Heshbon.' The prayer joins Deuteronomy 2:7 and 2:24-36 exactly as Moses did, provision followed by victory.

God reminds Israel that He brought 'the Philistines from Caphtor, and the Arameans from Kir.' Amos takes up the principle of Deuteronomy 2:10-23: the migrations of other nations are also God's work, so Israel's election is grace, not a claim that God cares only for them.

Paul tells the Athenians that God 'determined their appointed times and the boundaries of their lands' so that they would seek Him. Deuteronomy 2 shows that truth in miniature, as God assigns lands to Edom, Moab and Ammon, and Acts gives its purpose.

Paul quotes God's word to Pharaoh and concludes, 'He hardens whom He wants to harden.' The hardening of Sihon in Deuteronomy 2:30 belongs to the same pattern, and Paul uses it to show that God's purposes of mercy are carried out even through human resistance.

study.oneStory:
In the story of Scripture, Deuteronomy 2 marks the turn from judgment to fulfilment. Genesis 12 promised that through Abraham all the families of the earth would be blessed, and Genesis 15 promised his descendants a land once the iniquity of the Amorites was complete. Chapter 1 showed how unbelief delayed that promise. Chapter 2 shows the delay ending. The last of the Kadesh generation dies, the Zered is crossed, and the first Amorite king falls.

The chapter also shows that God's story was never only about Israel. The notes on Edom, Moab and Ammon, and even on the Caphtorites, place Israel in a crowded world where God is at work among many peoples. That wider horizon runs back to the table of nations in Genesis 10 and forward to the prophets who promise restoration for Moab and Ammon, Jeremiah 48:47 and 49:6.

It sets up what comes next in two ways. The defeat of Sihon, and of Og in chapter 3, gives Israel a pattern for the conquest of Canaan, which Moses and Rahab both point to. And the restraint toward Esau and Lot sets a boundary on the conquest, which is not a license for unlimited expansion but the receiving of a particular gift.

The story comes to its centre in Christ, through whom God's care for the nations becomes a gospel for the nations. The peace offered to Sihon is offered to the world, the hostile powers are overthrown at the cross, and the boundaries of the nations become the fields into which the good news runs.

The new creation completes the picture. John sees the nations walking by the light of the Lamb, and 'the glory and honor of the nations' brought into the city, Revelation 21:24-26. The peoples whose borders God guarded on Israel's journey are gathered, and the judgment that fell on the hardened is finished, so that the people of God can finally lack nothing forever.

quiz.q: Why did the LORD tell Israel not to provoke Edom, Moab, or Ammon (vv.5, 9, 19)?

options.text: Because He had already given each of those lands to their respective descendants as a possession.
options.note: All three passages give this exact reason: God had already granted these lands to Esau's and Lot's descendants.

options.text: Because Israel was too weak to fight them.
options.note: The text gives no indication of weakness; the reason given is God's prior land grant to these peoples.

options.text: Because Israel had signed treaties with them.
options.note: No treaty is mentioned; the restriction comes directly from the LORD's command.

options.text: Because those nations posed no threat at all.
options.note: Verse 4 notes they were afraid of Israel, showing Israel could have threatened them; the restraint was commanded, not circumstantial.

quiz.q: What happened to the earlier inhabitants of the lands later held by Moab, Ammon, and Edom (vv.10-12, 20-23)?

options.text: They too were displaced by the LORD's providence, just as Israel would displace the Canaanites.
options.note: The parenthetical notes describe the Emites, Zamzummites, Horites, and Avvim all being destroyed or displaced before these nations settled the land.

options.text: They were peacefully absorbed into these nations.
options.note: The text describes destruction and displacement, not peaceful absorption.

options.text: They still lived there at the time of Moses' address.
options.note: Verse 22 specifically notes the earlier peoples were destroyed 'to this day', meaning they were long gone by Moses' time.

options.text: The text says nothing happened to them.
options.note: Verses 10-12, 20-23 describe their fate in detail.

quiz.q: What reason does verse 30 give for Sihon's refusal to let Israel pass through peacefully?

options.text: The LORD had made his spirit stubborn and his heart obstinate so He might deliver him into Israel's hand.
options.note: This is exactly what verse 30 states, echoing the hardening of Pharaoh's heart.

options.text: Sihon simply loved war for its own sake.
options.note: No such personal motive is given; the text attributes the hardening to the LORD's purpose.

options.text: Sihon feared losing his throne to a rival king.
options.note: No such political threat is mentioned in the text.

options.text: No reason is given for his refusal.
options.note: Verse 30 gives an explicit theological reason.

quiz.q: What happened to the cities of Sihon's kingdom after Israel defeated him (v.34)?

options.text: They were devoted to destruction, including women and children, with no survivors left.
options.note: Verse 34 states this plainly and starkly.

options.text: They were spared and resettled peacefully by Israel.
options.note: The text describes total destruction, not peaceful resettlement.

options.text: They surrendered without any fighting.
options.note: Verse 32 describes Sihon coming out for battle at Jahaz; there was real combat.

options.text: Israel avoided those cities entirely.
options.note: Verse 34 says Israel captured all of Sihon's cities.

quiz.q: How long did Israel's journey take from Kadesh-barnea until they crossed the Brook of Zered (v.14)?

options.text: Thirty-eight years, until that whole generation of fighting men had perished.
options.note: Verse 14 gives this exact figure and reason.

options.text: Eleven days.
options.note: Eleven days is the length of the direct route from Horeb to Kadesh-barnea mentioned in 1:2, not this later span.

options.text: Forty years exactly.
options.note: The total wilderness period is forty years, but this specific span from Kadesh-barnea to the Brook of Zered is thirty-eight.

options.text: Two years.
options.note: The text specifies thirty-eight years, not two.

questions: God set firm boundaries even for nations outside His covenant, giving Edom, Moab, and Ammon their own land. What does it teach you about God's character that His sovereign care extends even to people outside 'His people'?
Sihon's stubborn heart still served God's larger purpose, even in open opposition. Where might God be turning someone's resistance, or even your own past resistance, toward His purposes?

Israel had to wait thirty-eight years, watching a whole generation pass away, before this new chapter of victory could begin. Where are you in a season of waiting that feels wasted, and how might God still be at work in it?

Israel was told plainly not to provoke Edom, Moab, or Ammon and to accept the limits God had set. Where do you need to accept a limit God has placed rather than reaching for what is not yours to take?
Moses reminds Israel, 'you have lacked nothing' even in the wilderness. Where have you overlooked God's provision during a season that felt like aimless wandering?

translationNotes.note: These parenthetical historical notes would have been common knowledge to Moses' original audience; they explain that the displacement Israel is about to carry out against the Canaanites already has precedent in how Edom, Moab, and Ammon obtained their own lands.
The figure of thirty-eight years ties this account directly to the forty-year sentence pronounced in Numbers 14, marking this as the tail end of that period of judgment.

'Hardened his spirit' uses language that closely mirrors the hardening of Pharaoh's heart in Exodus, signaling a recurring biblical pattern of God's sovereign purpose working through real human stubbornness.
